# Where to Begin {#sec-closing}

The book opened with a case: drug-sensitivity signatures,
used to assign patients to treatment arms, that rested on
analyses no one could re-run. Two statisticians
reconstructed the analyses from the outside and found
simple errors (@sec-intro). Every chapter since has
supplied part of the remedy. This closing chapter gathers
the argument into four points and turns it into a plan a
student can start this week. It ends with a page that a
student can hand to a supervisor who has not read the
book.

## The argument in four points {#sec-conclusion}

The book's argument comes down to four points.
Reproducibility, we have maintained throughout,
is not a badge a project either holds or lacks. It is a
level a project reaches. The discipline is to reach as
high as the work warrants and to say plainly how high
that was.

First, reproducibility comes in degrees, and the ladder
names them: locatable (L0), pinned packages (L1), pinned
environment (L2), and verified (L3). Every chapter of
this book has been an ascent of that ladder. We began by
finding the source and pinning the packages with a
lockfile. We then fixed the environment with a container
or a content-addressed alternative, and finally
regenerated the outputs and confirmed they match. The
ladder is the common scale on which any analysis, built
with any toolchain, can be placed and compared.

Second, the rungs are reached by two different kinds of
work, and conflating them is the source of much
confusion. Capture fixes the inputs and sets the level
from L0 to L2. Pinning the packages and the environment
is capture, which carries a compendium as far as L2. The
last rung, L3, is reached not by capture but by an act
of verification: a clean rebuild after which a baseline
test passes within a stated tolerance. Running that
verification once, with such a baseline test in place
(in the book's framework, `zzc verify`), is therefore
what lifts a pinned L2 compendium to a verified L3 one.
Automated re-checking is distinct from that act.
Continuous integration reruns the verification on every
change and certifies that the L3 state still holds, but
it adds no rung of its own. Removing it does not lower
the level; it only stops the automated confirmation.
Keeping these registers distinct is what lets a project
report, honestly and mechanically, exactly where it
stands.

Third, the unit of reproducible work is the research
compendium, and it is not only a manuscript. The same
machinery, the same pillars, and the same ladder serve a
data analysis, a simulation study, an R package, a blog,
and a scholarly manuscript alike. The archetypes differ
only in their directory layout, in whether a report is
rendered, and in the last mile of publication: a package
submission, a deployed website, or a deposit beside an
article.

Fourth, and above all, the goal is reproducibility
matched honestly to the level actually reached. The
tools this book has taught, and the framework it has used
as its running example, are strong but partial. They
firmly secure some determinants and leave others to
convention, and an honest practitioner discloses the
difference. A verified L3 compendium and a locatable L0
script are both legitimate outputs of a scientific
process; what is not legitimate is to present the second
as the first. The reader who finishes this book with the
judgment to name the level a given analysis has reached,
across whatever archetype the work takes, and the
honesty to claim no more, has learned the one thing the
book most wished to teach.

## A plan for your own project

A book this long can leave the impression that the
practices arrive all at once. They do not, and they
should not. The order below follows the ladder, and each
step is useful on its own if the next never comes. The
time labels are suggestions for a student starting a
thesis project, not measurements.

**This week: make the project locatable (L0).** Put the
analysis under version control and push it to a private
remote (@sec-version-control). Add a README that says
what the project is, where the data come from, and how
to run the analysis. Keep raw data out of the history
from the first commit, with a `.gitignore` written before
any data arrive.

**This month: pin the packages (L1).** Initialize `renv`,
take a snapshot when the analysis runs cleanly, and
commit the lockfile (@sec-dependencies). Move file paths
to project-relative form, and replace every typed number
in the report with an inline expression
(@sec-literate). Record the R version the analysis uses.

**Before the first submission: pin the environment and
check it (L2, then L3).** Write a Dockerfile, or choose
an alternative backend if Docker is not available
(@sec-containers, @sec-backends). Add a baseline test
that compares the main estimates with recorded values
within a stated tolerance (@sec-testing). Run the
verification once on a clean machine, then let
continuous integration repeat it on every change
(@sec-verification).

**At publication: deposit and disclose.** Archive the
compendium with a persistent identifier, cite the
version used, and state in the article the level the
analysis actually reached (@sec-archiving). Where the
data cannot be shared, say how they can be obtained and
share everything else.

Not every project needs every step. An exploratory
analysis that will never be published may rightly stop
at L1. The judgment that @sec-levels asks of every
analyst is the same one this plan asks of its reader:
climb as far as the stakes warrant, and say where the
climb stopped.

## For your supervisor: one page

A supervisor who has published for years without these
practices is entitled to ask what they cost and what
they buy. The following page is written to be handed
over as it stands.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Reproducible analysis: a one-page brief

**What is proposed.** The student's analysis will be
kept under version control, with its package versions
recorded, and, before submission, run once more from a
clean start to confirm that the published numbers
regenerate. Nothing in the statistical analysis changes.

**What it protects against.** Analyses fail to re-run
far more often than is usually assumed. Of more than
nine thousand R files deposited with published articles,
roughly one in four ran without error
[@trisovic2022]. Errors that survive into print are
usually simple. Genomic analyses used to assign patients
to treatment arms rested on errors as plain as shifted
rows [@baggerly2009]. A published clinical trial was
retracted and republished with its two arms' results
exchanged, reversing its conclusion [@aboumatar2019]. Each was found only because
someone could re-run or inspect the computation.

**What it costs.** The first steps, version control and
a recorded list of package versions, add little to the
work and change nothing in the analysis. The later steps
are taken only where the stakes of the project warrant
them.

**What it buys the laboratory.** A reviewer's request
for a re-analysis can be answered without rebuilding
anything. A student's departure does not take the
analysis with it. And the project meets the data- and
code-sharing requirements that funders and journals
increasingly impose (@tbl-mandates).

**What is asked of the supervisor.** Nothing beyond
tolerance for the student's own project. Further steps
can wait until the first ones have proved their worth.
:::

## When your laboratory does not work this way yet

Most students who adopt these practices do so in a group
that has not. That is no obstacle to starting, because
every step in the plan above can be taken on one
person's project without changing anyone else's. Three
observations may help.

First, practice spreads by example more than by
argument. A student whose figures regenerate on request,
whose analysis survives a change of laptop, and whose
code a newcomer can run, demonstrates the case more
persuasively than any chapter of this book.

Second, the parts that touch other people deserve
care. Restricted data are governed by agreements the
student did not write (@sec-archiving), and a
laboratory's shared resources, such as a common image or
a shared repository, belong to the group. Propose those
changes rather than make them.

Third, the case should be made in the supervisor's
terms, not the book's. A supervisor in clinical research
may respond to the trial whose arms were exchanged, and an
economist to the spreadsheet behind the debt threshold.
Anyone running a long pipeline may respond to the
operating systems that changed brain scans (@sec-crisis). The four
objections that @sec-four-objections answers are the
ones most likely to be raised.
